title: Andy Burnham’s Neet dilemma
gist: Labour peer Andrew Adonis backs Andy Burnham's post-14 vocational push (modelled on the Manchester MBacc) but rejects the premise that too many British teenagers are lured to university: the real drain is disengagement from schooling altogether, with over a quarter of secondary pupils missing more than 10 per cent of classes and about a third leaving without a Grade 4 in GCSE English and maths. He argues Britain has been recycling the same technical-education diagnosis since an 1884 royal commission, and that curriculum reform fails without a big expansion of youth apprenticeships and direct work on school attendance.

insights.claim: A British royal commission on technical education in 1884 already recommended making the UK's schooling and workplace training more like Germany's, 142 years before Andy Burnham's 2026 announcement of vocational routes for over-14s.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
entities: royal commission on British technical education
insights.so_what: UK skills policy is a repeat-announcement market: treat each new vocational initiative as low-probability of structural change unless it comes with delivery machinery, not just curriculum wording.
insights.quote: One hundred and forty-two years before Andy Burnham’s announcement this week that he will introduce more vocational education for over-14s, a royal commission on British technical education, under Queen Victoria, recommended reforms to make Britain more like Germany in its schooling and workplace training.
insights.locator: One hundred and forty-two years before

insights.claim: The one substantive change since 1884 is that critics no longer call British education inadequate in its entirety — they instead blame an oversupply of university places, which is a different and weaker diagnosis.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: The framing shift matters politically: policy aimed at shrinking universities addresses a symptom the data does not support, so expect misallocated reform effort.
insights.quote: The 1884 royal commission criticised British education as chronically inadequate in its entirety.
insights.locator: Actually, one big thing has changed

themes.theme: Against the 'too many go to university' consensus

insights.claim: The claim that the social magnetism of higher education has crowded out vocational routes is a zero-sum fallacy — expanding vocational education does not require doing down universities.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Signals an intra-Labour split on how to fund and frame skills policy; university-exposed assets (student housing, edtech, international recruitment) face rhetorical rather than fundamental risk from the Burnham agenda.
insights.quote: I don’t buy that “rob Peter to pay Paul” bit of the argument.
insights.locator: I don’t buy that “rob Peter to pay Paul”

insights.claim: The UK's university system is a world-class national asset funded largely by graduates themselves, who mostly do well in the jobs market, making it one of the world's top destinations for international students and researchers.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Frames higher education as an export sector worth defending — relevant to any policy shock to international student visas or fee regimes.
insights.quote: There is a reason why the UK is one of the world’s top destinations for international students and researchers.
insights.locator: It is a huge national strength

insights.claim: British universities are in serious financial crisis and have become too expensive largely because the Cameron-Clegg coalition trebled tuition fees and then levied a high interest rate on student debt on top.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Points to fee and student-loan interest reform, not headcount cuts, as the live policy lever on the university funding gap.
insights.quote: In particular, they have become too expensive, thanks largely to the misguided decision of the Cameron-Clegg coalition to treble tuition fees, and then to levy a high interest rate on student debt on top of that.

insights.claim: Even after higher education expansion and the achievement of Tony Blair's 50 per cent participation target, more than half of each year's cohort of British school leavers still do not go to university.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: The addressable market for vocational and apprenticeship provision is the majority of each cohort, not a residual — sizeable and structurally underserved.
insights.quote: it is still the case that more than half of each year’s cohort of school leavers don’t go on to university
insights.locator: However, even with the expansion of higher education

themes.theme: Attendance and attainment collapse as the real Neet driver

insights.claim: The dangerous magnet pulling working-class British teenagers away from vocational routes is opting out of education entirely, not the glamour of student life.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Reframes the Neet problem as an engagement and attendance failure, which implies spending on outreach and children's services rather than on rebalancing post-18 places.
insights.quote: The dangerous magnet attracting working-class teenagers isn’t higher education, but rather opting out of education entirely.
insights.locator: It is a thoroughly wrong-headed, upper-middle-class view

insights.claim: More than a quarter of English secondary school students are recorded as missing more than 10 per cent of their classes, with absenteeism having risen dramatically during the Covid pandemic and remaining alarmingly high.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Persistent post-Covid absence is a hard leading indicator for the future Neet cohort and UK labour-force participation.
insights.quote: More than a quarter of secondary school students are recorded as missing more than 10 per cent of their classes.
insights.locator: Rates of absenteeism from secondary schools

insights.claim: About a third of British school leavers fail to get a Grade 4 or above in GCSE English and maths, leaving school with few if any worthwhile qualifications.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A third of each cohort is functionally unqualified at 16 — the binding constraint on any UK skills or productivity uplift story.
insights.quote: About a third fail to get a Grade 4 or above in GCSE English and maths, which means that they leave school with few if any worthwhile qualifications.
insights.locator: About a third fail to get a Grade 4

insights.claim: The share of British school leavers failing to achieve basic qualifications is roughly the same — above one-third — as the share going on to university, which makes it nonsensical to blame school failure on the pull of higher education.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: A clean numerical rebuttal to the anti-university skills argument; useful when assessing the durability of policy proposals to cap university numbers.
insights.quote: It is completely nonsensical to think that this crisis of school failure is caused by too many pupils being too attracted to higher education.
insights.locator: Just pause on those figures for a moment

themes.theme: MBacc design and the apprenticeship bottleneck

insights.claim: Burnham's model, based on the Manchester MBacc, has schools offering GCSE or BTEC options in engineering, AI and other digital tech, art and design and health and social care alongside English, maths and science after age 14.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: AI and digital tech being written into 14-16 curriculum options creates a downstream pipeline and a procurement market for training providers and edtech.
insights.locator: Far better school-level vocational education options after the age of 14

insights.claim: A large increase in the number and quality of youth apprenticeships is the key requirement for post-14 vocational reform, because it is what gives school leavers a tangible and immediate route into employment.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Curriculum change without employer-funded apprenticeship places will not move Neet numbers — watch levy reform and employer commitments as the real signal.
insights.quote: A key requirement is a huge increase in the number and quality of youth apprenticeships.

insights.claim: Work experience should be systematically organised for pupils while they are still in secondary school, not left until after they leave.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: Implies an employer-engagement obligation that would fall on UK firms — a modest cost line but a recruiting channel for sectors with labour shortages.
insights.quote: Further, we should be systematically organising work experience for pupils while they are still in secondary school.
insights.locator: Further, we should be systematically organising

insights.claim: Making secondary school more relevant through vocational options only partly addresses working-class teenage disengagement; the more basic challenge is schools working directly with parents and children's services agencies to get teenagers into school at all.
insights.speaker: Andrew Adonis
insights.so_what: The binding fix sits in social services capacity, not education policy — a spending pressure that competes with curriculum funding.
insights.quote: But there is a more basic challenge here, which is for schools to work directly with parents and children’s services agencies in order to get teenagers to go to school in the first place.
insights.locator: But there is a more basic challenge here
